title: How Hate Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore hate: how it differs from everyday dislike and from anger, Aristotle's definition, a 2008 University College London brain study (seventeen people, fMRI, putamen and insular cortex versus frontal cortex activity), whether hate is ancient or learned, Carthage and Rome and the Italian vendetta, Nazi propaganda and Martin Oppenheimer's analysis of scapegoating, a 2010 Stanford study on teaching teenagers to hate through stories, D. W. Griffith's Birth of a Nation and Nazi film Jud Süß, media and online hate (Bosnian Serb TV series, Facebook, neo-Nazi music), whether hate is a mental illness, a Kosovo trauma study, hate crime law, Southern Poverty Law Center state rankings, and a listener email on suicide bombing and asymmetry of power.
topics: suicide bombing and asymmetry of power

segments.title: Opening banter and the word hate
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about things they hate, such as broccoli and split peas, then note that people use the word hate casually. A University of Texas study found people rarely hate every day.

segments.title: Hate versus anger and types of hate
segments.summary: Aristotle's definition of hate is discussed as a dislike based on a negative perception of someone's nature that leads one to want to cause harm. The hosts distinguish casual hate from fear-based group hate and from anger-based retribution. They debate whether hate and anger are the same, with one view holding that hate comes from humiliation or devaluation and anger from perceived unfairness.

segments.title: Hate, frustration and the fascist scapegoat
segments.summary: The hosts link hate to frustration and displaced anger, noting that fascism directs group frustration at a scapegoat. They discuss anger and hate as intertwined emotions and the basic emotions debate.

segments.title: Brain study of love and hate
segments.summary: The hosts describe a 2008 University College London study of seventeen people who hated someone. Under fMRI, the putamen and insular cortex fired for pictures of hated people, the same regions that fire for loved ones. Frontal cortex judgment areas became less active for loved ones but stayed active for hated people. The hosts criticize the small, narrow sample.

segments.title: Serial killers and cold hatred
segments.summary: The hosts argue that calm, detached hatred is more dangerous than hot passion. They discuss whether serial killers hate their victims and how antisocial personality disorder figures into research.

segments.title: Evolutionary origins of hate
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether hate is ancient, citing the brain's older structures and the newer prefrontal cortex. They suggest hate may have evolved as a survival tool for hunter-gatherers to justify taking resources from other groups. Josh says he believes everyone has a capacity to hate but that people are not generally hateful.

segments.title: Hannibal, Rome, and the vendetta
segments.summary: Hannibal of Carthage is said to have sworn hatred of Rome as a boy. The hosts discuss Roman cruelty toward Carthaginians and whether hate actually drives war. They mention religious condemnations of hatred and the Italian vendetta, and the Latin term inimicitia for legal enmity.

segments.title: Nazi propaganda, media and online hate
segments.summary: The hosts describe Martin Oppenheimer's view that the Nazis showed how to stir group hate by exploiting frustration over unemployment. They discuss how cults and extremist groups target marginalized people, and a 2010 Stanford study on telling stories to teach teenagers to hate. They cover D. W. Griffith's Birth of a Nation, Nazi film Jud Süß, a Bosnian Serb TV series, and online hate on chat rooms, Facebook and neo-Nazi music.

segments.title: Mental illness, hate crime law and hate group statistics
segments.summary: The hosts ask whether hate is a mental illness, citing Hitler, bin Laden and the Columbine shooters, and mention a 2000s study of Kosovars showing that those who suffered the most trauma hated Serbian troops. They summarize hate crime laws that cover disability and sexual orientation, and the Southern Poverty Law Center's ranking of states with the most hate groups, led by Montana.

segments.title: Listener mail on suicide bombing and power asymmetry
segments.summary: A listener named Nick writes that suicide bombing often arises where there is a large power imbalance between an occupier and a weaker group, citing Vietnamese and Tamil Tiger examples, which the hosts agree is an important point.
